name: Mungkip
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.citation: Retsema, Thom, Margaret Potter and Rachel Gray. 2009. Mungkip: an endangered language. SIL Electronic Survey Report 2009-015. Dallas: SIL International. 35 pp.
sources.note: Sec. 4.1 (pp. 7-9) gives consonant and vowel phone charts from a 170-item wordlist; the only mention of stress is that [ɛ] is commoner in unstressed and [e] in stressed syllables (p. 9) -- no statement of where stress falls; authors say a thorough phonological analysis was not possible (p. 7); appendix wordlist transcriptions (pp. 11ff, checked visually) carry length/half-length marks but no stress marks.
Lexical database only; lists McElhanon & Voorhoeve (1970) and Retsema et al. (2009) as the sole sources for Mungkip; no prosodic information.

sources.citation: McElhanon, K. A. 1973. Towards a typology of the Finisterre-Huon languages, New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics B-22. Canberra: ANU. 92 pp.
sources.harvard_location: DIV Offsite Storage - Ask at Circulation (Pamph. folio) BS 354.Z91
sources.note: Ch. 1 Phonology (pp. 5-7) tabulates phonemes, syllable structure and morphophonemics for ten representative languages (Uri represents Erap; Munkip only appears in the family list and a lexicostatistic remark); no stress statement at all, none for Munkip.

sources.citation: Claassen, Oren R. and Kenneth A. McElhanon. 1970. Languages of the Finisterre Range - New Guinea. Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 11 (Pacific Linguistics A-23), 45-78. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Sec. 2.7.7 is one paragraph locating Munkip village (pop. 100) and its lexical affinities; sec. 6.1 Phonology gives Finisterre-Stock generalities and says stress is phonemic in Rawa, probably sub-phonemic in Yupna and Wantoat, contrastive on few words in Suroi -- nothing on Munkip stress.

sources.citation: Potter, Margaret, Rachel Gray and Thom Retsema. 2008. Nakame [nib] language survey report. Manuscript. Ukarumpa: SIL-PNG. (cited in ESR 2009-015; Mungkip is lexically close enough to Nakame to be 'considered a dialect of Nakame')
